messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mara is a 33-year-old graphic designer of European descent who lives with her husband in a mid-sized American city. She was referred for psychological assessment following eighteen months of progressively worsening anxiety, hypervigilance, and social withdrawal that she traces directly to a sustained stalking campaign carried out by a former colleague. For nearly eight months, this individual followed her home from work on multiple occasions, sent unsolicited messages, appeared outside her apartment building, and on one occasion trailed her on his bicycle through several city blocks as she rode home in the early evening — close enough that she could hear the rhythm of his wheels on the pavement behind her. She reported the behaviour to her employer and to the police, but no formal charges were ever filed and the man was quietly transferred to another department. The case was, in every practical sense, closed without consequence.

In the weeks that followed the stalking, Mara found herself unable to ride her bicycle — once a daily pleasure and her primary commute — without a cold certainty that someone was behind her. The sound of a bicycle approaching from the rear, a figure drawing close on the pavement, or the simple sensation of another person walking at her pace would immediately activate a surge of alarm: her heart would accelerate, her breathing would shallow, and she would begin scanning doorways and side streets for a way out. These triggers reliably produced what she described as a full-body sense of threat, as though her nervous system had concluded the danger was still ongoing. She became easily startled by ordinary sounds — a door closing, footsteps in a corridor — and she had begun mentally cataloguing exits before entering any room, a habit she initially experienced as prudent and now recognises as exhausting.

The absence of any accountability for her stalker had settled into something deeper than frustration. Mara had come to believe, with quiet conviction, that the world was genuinely dangerous and that people were rarely what they appeared to be. Colleagues who seemed friendly struck her as potentially deceptive; strangers who glanced at her in a coffee shop felt like threats. These appraisals did not remain abstract — they fed directly into her vigilance, amplifying the threat she perceived in ordinary situations and making the triggers she encountered at work and in daily life feel more charged. As a graphic designer who frequently works from cafés and shared studio spaces, she now enters every new environment already scanning for exits and positioning herself against walls, her back to the room. The belief that no one could be trusted made her reluctant to ask colleagues to walk with her to the car park, so the checking and the positioning became her private, solitary system of protection.

Over months, the strategies that were meant to keep her safe began to sustain the very fear they were designed to manage. Constantly scanning her surroundings meant she was perpetually finding things to scan — a man standing too long near the entrance, a bicycle locked outside that had not been there before — and each sweep of the environment renewed the sense that danger was present. Staying near exits meant she never fully settled anywhere, and her body never received the signal that she was safe. Her husband noticed she had stopped attending social events and had asked to work from home on days when she would normally have cycled to the studio; she told him she was tired, but what she was actually doing was avoiding the street where the stalking had most frequently occurred. The avoidance had narrowed her life considerably, and the narrowing had, in its own way, confirmed her belief that the world outside was something to be managed rather than inhabited. The strategies that felt like control were quietly reinforcing the appraisals that made control feel necessary, and the appraisals in turn made her more sensitive to the very triggers she was trying to avoid.

Mara sought help after her husband gently observed that she had not ridden her bicycle in over a year and that she flinched when someone knocked at their front door. What brought her into the consulting room was less any single incident than the accumulated weight of a life organised around threat. She hopes, cautiously, to feel safe enough to cycle to work again. What she fears most is that she never will — and that, somewhere, the person responsible is simply living his life unchanged.
